title_original: Photo Days Opens the Doors Paris Keeps Shut
excerpt_original: For its seventh edition, the photography festival takes the designer agnès b. as its godmother and lets itself into the most discreet addresses of Paris and greater Paris. L’article Photo Days Opens the Doors Paris Keeps Shut est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .

blocks.text: November in Paris belongs to photography. Paris Photo, the international fair installed at the Grand Palais since 1997, keeps the beat. But another fixture has claimed a place on the calendar since 2020: Photo Days, which spends the entire month gathering galleries, museums and landmark buildings around contemporary work.

“What really defines Photo Days is that we move into places that are not exhibition spaces,” says Emmanuelle de l’Ecotais, art historian, former head of the photography collection at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, and the woman behind the project. The festival hands each artist a carte blanche and asks them to talk back to the walls. “We never use a space as a white cube.”

blocks.caption: Photo Days · MAC Créteil © Véronique Ellena, Soleil, série Mains d’œuvre, 2025-2026 · courtesy Hangar Gallery, Bruxelles

blocks.text: This edition, which falls on the medium’s bicentennial, has a godmother for the first time. One name came immediately: agnès b. She opened Galerie du Jour in 1986, and it has taken part in the festival from the beginning. “Everyone knows her collection. Very few people know that she is a photographer herself,” the artistic director goes on. “The photographs you see on her clothes are her own.”

For the occasion, the designer opens the doors of the Maison agnès b., at 17 rue Dieu in the 10th arrondissement, long enough to hang a group of her own photographs, taken in Moscow in 1987. The rest of the year the public does not get in. That is this festival’s particular gift, to venture into a Paris that is almost secret.
A Rotunda, a Chapel, a Corridor

The festival’s first improbable venue began with a refusal. In 2020, for its inaugural edition, Emmanuelle de l’Ecotais approached the Fondation des Artistes about the Hôtel Salomon de Rothschild. “They laughed in my face, very kindly,” she recalls. The reasoning was unanswerable. The mansion rents itself out for private events, and the proceeds keep the Maison nationale des artistes going, the nursing home the foundation maintains at Nogent-sur-Marne for aging artists.

What she was offered instead was rarer still: the Rotonde Balzac, “a sort of little jewel set down in the middle of the garden.” Commissioned around 1890 by the Baroness de Rothschild, it rises on the remains of a pavilion built by the architect Eugène Monnier for Count Mniszech, the writer’s son-in-law, whose house once stood nearby. Cross the threshold and you find an orientalist interior reassembled from Monnier’s drawings, with panels of embroidered gauze and carved wainscoting of basketry, facing dragons and serpents.

blocks.caption: Photo Days · Rotonde Balzac © Alexandra Catiere, Salve, 2026
Photo Days · Rotonde Balzac © Alexandra Catiere, Salve, 2026

blocks.text: Every autumn since, an artist has had to come to terms with Balzac. The photographer Alexandra Catiere, who won this year’s Balzac & le vin commission and the Prix Niépce Gens d’images, shows “Salve” there. She takes her cue from Balzac’s Eugénie Grandet and from the Romantic ritual of contemplating the sky at an agreed hour, then photographs the evening vault herself at nine o’clock, layering analog processes to summon memory and attachment. She passes the instruction along to her visitors, who are invited to raise their glasses as readily as their eyes, and to photograph the sky in their turn, in honor of the people they love.

The festival also takes up quarters on rue de Sèvres, in the chapel of Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, the Lazarist mother house that holds the relics of its founder. Thomas Klotz, who practiced law before turning to the large-format view camera, shows “Révélation” there, the product of a year spent among that community and the one at the chapel of the Miraculous Medal on rue du Bac, kept by the Daughters of Charity, the other congregation Vincent de Paul founded. The hang runs well past the nave. “We go all the way into the refectory. You see where the sisters and the fathers live from day to day.”

blocks.text: At the Sorbonne, in the Galerie Soufflot of the Centre Panthéon, Catherine Balet takes over the old display cases where examination results were once posted. Outside the commissioned shows, the artistic director takes on the guest curatorship of “Humanité” at the Centre Tchèque de Paris. Inside hang some eighty silver gelatin prints by Jindřich Štreit, a self-taught Czech photographer who spent the 1990s photographing, with great tenderness, the inhabitants of overlooked regions in Bohemia and northern France.

The full program runs to 72 exhibitions and more than 230 artists, from the major institutions — the Maison Européenne de la Photographie, Le Bal, the Fondation Henri Cartier-Bresson — to some 20 partner galleries. Emmanuelle de l’Ecotais slips two favorites into the mix. The first is Elizabeth Lennard, an American photographer and filmmaker settled in Paris, who has been working over her own images since the 1970s; one of them became this year’s poster. She is showing on rue de Seine at Galerie Pixi, opened in 1990 by Serge Poliakoff’s granddaughter.

blocks.caption: Photo Days · Pixi © Elizabeth Lennard, Tom’s Luncheonette New York, 1980
Photo Days · Pixi © Elizabeth Lennard, Toy Noy New York, 1980

blocks.text: The second is Payram, “an absolutely magnificent artist,” a master printer by trade who spent his career at the legendary Picto lab. At Maubert, in the Marais, he hangs portraits of his fellow exiles, the ones who fled Iran as he did and who have been sitting for him for more than thirty years. He photographs them on a view camera loaded with Polaroid film, then prints on baryta paper, sometimes solarizing.

The program spills well past the Périphérique, out to the Maison des Arts in Créteil, where Véronique Ellena devotes “Mains d’œuvre” to apprentices at a vocational training center. All that is left is to choose where to begin. The festival, for its part, says as much at the bottom of its poster: “There’s no escaping photography.”

blocks.text: The 7th edition of Photo Days runs from November 2 to November 30, 2026, in Paris and the Île-de-France. Several of the exhibitions mentioned here fall outside those dates: – “5 jours à Moscou en 1987” at the Maison agnès b. (17 rue Dieu) through November 13, 2026; – “Salve” by Alexandra Catiere at the Rotonde Balzac through November 28, 2026 (by appointment); – “Mains d’œuvre” by Véronique Ellena at the Maison des Arts de Créteil through December 19, 2026; – “Que vos pas soient légers, car vous marchez sur mes rêves” (Tread softly because you tread on my dreams) by Payram at Galerie Maubert through January 9, 2027; – “Humanité” by Jindřich Štreit at the Centre Tchèque de Paris through January 16, 2027. The full program is available here .
